title: Recruiting Emails: 20 Experiments, 200 Roles (November 2026)
summary: A look back at 20 recruiting email experiments across 200 roles, with November 2026 context on testing and deliverability.
body_markdown:
Low interest rates on outbound[recruiting emails](https://www.dover.com/) leave hiring teams with a choice: rewrite copy by instinct, send more volume, or test individual elements like subject line, structure, benefits, and links against a baseline. A study published in 2023, covering 20 experiments across 200 low-interest roles, took that approach. Below, which changes helped, which did not, and how far those findings should be trusted today.


**TLDR:**


- A vague subject line like “\[First Name\], looking for something new?” may lift interest rates.
- Concise bullet-point emails passing a single-scroll mobile test reported higher interest among respondents.
- Non-cash benefits and links to LinkedIn or job descriptions produced no consistent lift.
- Combining the winning subject line with bullet-point structure reported the largest gain.
- From a study published in 2023 of 20 experiments across 200 roles; treat as hypotheses, not current benchmarks.


## What We Thought Was Driving Low Interest


At the time of the study, we considered several possible causes of low interest, including unclear job descriptions, employer reputation, timing, and email copy. These were hypotheses behind the experiments, not proven explanations for the results, and the Great Resignation was part of that historical context rather than a description of today’s hiring market.


Each department pulled the levers it could. Marketing handled employer branding and cold outreach, while I, as content lead, focused on our autogenerated recruiting emails. We tried a few employer branding experiments too, but outreach was the lever we could scientifically measure, control, and maintain quality for, so that’s where I went all in.


## The Early Days of Dover Outreach


For current offerings only, Dover’s[current plan comparison](https://www.dover.com/pricing) lists a sourcing extension, email outreach campaigns, and campaign follow-ups on both Free and Premium. The original experiments compared changes to email copy against the automated candidate outreach used at the time, testing message variants rather than automation against human recruiters. The study describes repeated tests across role groups but does not provide the underlying response-level data or confidence intervals needed to independently check the reported gains.


## The Hypothesis


My goal was to see whether changing the email body could affect interest rates even when market conditions were outside our control. My hypothesis: **outreach copy could shape a candidate’s first impression of the opportunity.** A clearer, easier-to-scan message might change how candidates saw the same role without changing the job itself. Comparing copy variants within similar role groups and repeating the tests offered a way to check that idea.


## The Limitations


What appeals to one candidate might not appeal to all, so I wanted to use data to spot patterns and check for statistical significance. The experiments covered a selected group of low-interest roles, and nonresponses never revealed *why* a candidate declined to engage, leaving a few limitations:


1. Unclear whether candidates reacted to the **role** or the ***company*** .
2. Hard to separate company-specific copy from overall employer brand.
3. No way to know how many other emails a candidate received that day.


To control for this, I segmented subjects by role type, company size, and existing interest rate, and ran at least three iterations per experiment to validate results. HubSpot’s[A/B testing sample size guide](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/email-a-b-test-sample-size-testing-time) explains why sample size determines whether a difference is real or noise, which is the reason repeated tests matter for small role-level groups.


### So, What Did I Find?


For the most part, my instincts were wrong, which is exactly why we do research.


We’ll go over the 4 major experiment categories we tested, **plus a 5th experiment that combined the two winners** . The variables tested were subject lines, email structure (concise bullet points), non-cash benefits (like perks, stipends, and PTO), and links to LinkedIn profiles, websites, and job descriptions.


## The Experiments


### Study Mechanics


- **Who** : 200 roles with low interest rates (3% or lower than benchmark).
- **What:** Each study was an A/B test pitting our autogenerated outreach against the new variable being tested.
- **When** : Tests ran for two weeks each.
- **How** : Each experiment ran three to five iterations, with underperforming outliers sometimes moved into separate iterations to check for different results.
- **Controls** : Similar role types stayed grouped together in the same experiment to limit the variation discussed above.


*Historical recruiting email test results. Interest rate means interested replies divided by total replies, not total emails sent; these findings are not forecasts.*


Email change tested Reported result Limit when interpreting the result


Reading time or funding round in the subject line Negligible change in interest rate Neither variant produced a meaningful gain in these tests.


Less specific subject line: “\[First Name\], looking for something new?” 25% increase in interest rate across 80% of test subjects The study did not prove why this subject line performed better.


Concise bullet-point email structure Average interest rate of 1.35 times the baseline The ratio does not show an increase in opens, total replies, or hires.


Non-cash benefits in outreach No lift; lower interest in some cases Results varied across the tested roles.


Links to sender LinkedIn profiles, websites, and job descriptions No change across the test group Earlier one-off gains did not carry through to these tests.


Winning subject line combined with bullet-point structure More than 50% increase in interest rate The historical result does not predict performance for a new role or candidate pool.


## The Winners


### Experiment #1: Subject Lines


- **Test A:** Adding reading time to a subject line.
- **Test B:** Adding series funding to a subject line.
- **Test C** : Using a vague subject line: “\[First Name\], looking for something new?”
- **Results:** Test C won; Tests A and B were flat.


### The Takeaway


The vague subject line won here, but the study didn’t prove why.[Adobe’s A/B testing guidance](https://business.adobe.com/blog/basics/learn-about-a-b-testing) suggests changing one element at a time with similar audience groups, a way to check whether this still works for your candidate pool rather than assuming the old winner holds.


### Experiment #2: Bullet Point Structure - the Standout


- **What** : Rewrite outreach into concise bullet points and pass the “scroll” test on mobile, meaning the whole email fits in one scroll.
- **Results:** This variant reported an average interest rate above baseline, as shown in the results table.


### The Takeaway


Worth testing where long emails are hard to scan. The gain concerns interest among people who replied, not opens, total replies, or hires, and it doesn’t guarantee the same result for a different role or candidate pool. Litmus’s[email A/B testing guide](https://www.litmus.com/blog/email-ab-testing-how-to) notes that small samples rarely reach statistical significance, so repeat the test before trusting a winner.


## The Losers


### Experiment #3: Listing Non-Cash Benefits in Outreach


- **What** : With a crowded market, I wondered if[passive candidates](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-source-passive-candidates) would respond more to non-cash benefits than to job or company specifics.
- **Results: No lift, and lower interest in some cases.** Perks, stipends, and PTO were tested, but the report does not identify which benefit or role drove lower interest.


### Experiment #4: Linking to LinkedIn Profiles, Websites, and Job Descriptions


- **What** : Across the org, a few one-off variants had shown higher interest rates, so we tested the pattern here. One finding was that linking to the sender’s LinkedIn profile, the website, and the job description had slightly raised interest, maybe because candidates felt they were talking to a real person rather than an automation tool.
- **Results: Neutral, no change across the board.** Sometimes a fluke is a fluke.


## The Big Takeaway: Combining the Winners


### Experiment #5: Combining Winning Elements


- **What** : I combined the winning bullet-point template with the top subject line, “\[First Name\], looking for something new?”, to see if pairing the two winners produced an even greater lift.
- **Results:** Combining the bullet-point structure with the winning subject line increased interest rates in these historical tests, as shown in the results table.


Here’s the recipe to test across your open roles, and our guide to[writing better recruiting emails](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-write-great-recruiting-emails) for more on structure and tone.


**Template**


Hi {{FIRST_NAME}},


I’m {{HM}}, the {{role}} at {{company}}. {{Personalized_Content}} I thought you’d be a great addition to our team as a {{role}}.


Here’s a bit more about us and this opportunity:


- Mission statement
- Funding: $$ in Series X funding led by top investors: (list here)
- Being an early engineering hire means: adjective, adjective, adjective
- You’ll work with {{departments}}
- Tech stack (for eng), design program (for product)


If you’re interested, would you have 30 minutes in the next week to chat?


Best,
John Doe


## What Happened After


Overall, I learned that refreshing our outreach strategy, **running experiments, and testing new and creative types of content is key to staying competitive in a crowded hiring market.**


The original report described an A/B testing feature in the app at that time. That description is historical, not confirmation the same workflow is available today; Dover’s[current feature comparison](https://www.dover.com/pricing) lists email outreach campaigns and follow-ups, but not that specific workflow.


### Testing Recruiting Emails in October 2026


A copy test can mislead if delivery problems keep messages from reaching candidates. Google’s sender guidelines FAQ notes that Gmail began ramping up enforcement against noncompliant traffic in November 2025: SPF or DKIM authentication is now required for all senders to personal Gmail accounts, with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC required for bulk senders. Keeping the sending setup consistent across variants, checking delivery failures separately from replies, and tracking interested replies against total emails sent (alongside this study’s interest-among-respondents metric) helps separate copy performance from delivery problems and from a strong ratio among a small group of respondents.


### Applying the Findings Today


A historical winning template is a starting point, not a forecast; its value depends on whether it still performs for the role, audience, and message being tested. The lasting lesson is the test-and-repeat approach described in[Adobe’s experimentation guide](https://business.adobe.com/blog/basics/learn-about-a-b-testing) : a past winner is a reason to keep testing, not to stop.


## How Dover Fits Into Recruiting Email Testing


Dover’s free applicant tracking system offers some of the pieces a team can use to try the kind of tests described above. The sourcing extension sends email outreach campaigns directly from LinkedIn, campaigns can include follow-ups, and CRM and reporting dashboards track pipeline, sources, and hires, so each email version can be sent as its own outreach campaign and the results tracked in the same reporting.


Campaign size depends on the plan. The free tier adds one candidate at a time to a campaign, while uploading a CSV to send one campaign to many people is part of the Premium plan at $199 per month. Smaller tests on a single role can run free; larger tests across several roles may fit Premium better.


Someone still has to source candidates, write the variants, and read the results. A team hiring one or two roles with time to spare can often manage with the ATS alone. When roles are senior or specialized, or no one has recruiting bandwidth, a fractional recruiter from the Dover marketplace can take on sourcing and outreach inside Dover’s ATS.


## FAQs


### Should I add perks, PTO, or non-cash benefits to outbound recruiting emails?


In these experiments, non-cash benefits produced no consistent lift and lowered interest in some cases. The study didn’t identify which benefit or role drove the drop, so treat this as a reason to test, not a reason to skip benefits outright. Results may differ for your role and candidate pool.


### Can I combine Dover’s winning email template with my own outreach tools?


Yes. The bullet-point template and subject line format in this study can be tested in any outreach tool, including Dover, Greenhouse, Lever, or Ashby. The template is a copy framework, not a tool-specific feature, so the same test-and-repeat approach applies no matter which tool sends it.


### Do I need a recruiter if I already use an ATS to send outreach?


Not always. An ATS handles the system side: campaigns, follow-ups, tracking, and reporting on which variant performs better. A recruiter supplies capacity and judgment, like finding candidates, adjusting copy, and following up on replies. Teams with a few open roles can often manage with an ATS alone, while senior or specialized searches may benefit from a fractional recruiter working inside the same ATS, which helps avoid duplicate outreach.


## Final Thoughts on Turning Test Results Into a Repeatable Process


A historical winning template is a starting hypothesis. For[recruiting emails](https://www.dover.com/) , these results suggest that small changes to a subject line or email structure can move interest rates, while changes such as benefits or links may not. How well any of it holds up depends on the role, the candidate pool, and the delivery setup behind each send. Dover’s free ATS, with its sourcing extension, outreach campaigns, and reporting, is one place to send and track those outreach campaigns, with fractional recruiters available for teams that want hands-on help with the outreach itself.
